paragraphs.heading: Group 18
paragraphs.text: The noble gases make up group 18 of the periodic table: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon and, in some cases, oganesson. Under standard conditions the first six are gases made of single atoms, with no colour or smell and very low chemical reactivity. That reluctance to react comes from their electron arrangement: their outer shell of valence electrons is full. The properties of oganesson are uncertain.

paragraphs.heading: Weak forces, cold boiling points
paragraphs.text: Their atoms attract each other only through the very weak London dispersion force. As a result they boil only at extremely low temperatures, all below 165 K (−108 °C). They used to be called inert gases, but that label has been dropped because many noble gas compounds are now known. Even so, only a few hundred such compounds are known.

paragraphs.heading: Useful because they stay put
paragraphs.text: Because they hardly react, noble gases are handy wherever reactions are unwanted. Argon shields welds and fills incandescent light bulbs, and helium lifts blimps and balloons. Helium and neon also work as refrigerants, thanks to their low boiling points. All except radon are gathered in industrial amounts by liquefying air and separating it by fractional distillation. Radon is usually taken from the radioactive decay of radium, thorium or uranium compounds, and helium also comes from natural gas mining.

paragraphs.heading: A missing family
paragraphs.text: Helium was found on 18 August 1868 by Pierre Janssen and Joseph Norman Lockyer while studying the Sun's chromosphere, and named after the Greek word for the Sun. In 1895 Lord Rayleigh noticed that nitrogen taken from air had a different density from nitrogen made in chemical reactions. With William Ramsay he isolated the extra gas, argon, whose Greek name means idle or lazy. They realized a whole class of gases was absent from the periodic table, and in 1898 Ramsay found krypton, neon and xenon, named for the Greek words for hidden, new and stranger.

paragraphs.heading: Shaping ideas about the atom
paragraphs.text: In 1902 Mendeleev added helium and argon to his arrangement of the elements as group 0. Rayleigh and Ramsay won the 1904 Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry for finding the noble gases. Their discovery helped build a general understanding of atomic structure. In 1913 Niels Bohr proposed that electrons sit in shells around the nucleus, and that the outermost shell of every noble gas except helium holds eight electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Not so inert after all
paragraphs.text: In 1962 Neil Bartlett made xenon hexafluoroplatinate, the first known compound of any noble gas. Compounds of others came soon after: radon difluoride (RnF₂) in 1962 and krypton difluoride (KrF₂) in 1963. The first stable argon compound, argon fluorohydride (HArF), was reported in 2000, formed at just 40 K.
